pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of ANSWER)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of answer, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version, appearing in the Psalter's own recollections of prayer heard.
biblical_def:
Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God. In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.

Answeredst is the Psalter's word for prayer remembered as heard, never merely prayer offered. Psalm 99 recalls Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name; they called upon the LORD, and he answered them — a whole generation's leaders united by this one fact, that when they called, thou answeredst them. Psalm 138 turns the same word personal: in the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul, the answer not merely heard but felt, an inward strengthening alongside the outward deliverance. Both psalms hold answeredst together with a second, harder truth — that this same God who answers is also a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions (Psa 99:8), so that being answered never means being told sin carried no weight, only that grace outweighed it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ANSWER: to reply to a question, a call, or a prayer; here in the archaic second-person singular past, answeredst, addressed to thou in remembered prayer.
webster_full: ANSWER, v.t. To speak in return to a question, call, or argument.
ANSWER, v.t. To respond favorably; to grant what is desired, as in prayer.
ANSWEREDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as strengthenedst.
In Psalm 99 the word recalls a whole line of intercessors, Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, being heard.
In Psalm 138 the same word becomes personal testimony, paired with an inward strengthening.
scriptures: Psa 99:8
Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions.
In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic readings of answered prayer isolate the comfort of Psalm 138 from the sober balance of Psalm 99, where being answered stands alongside a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions — grace and holiness together, not grace as mere affirmation.
corruption_paragraphs: A sentimentalized reading of answered prayer wants Psalm 138's strengthenedst me with strength in my soul without Psalm 99's harder companion truth, that the same LORD who answers also took vengeance of their inventions — sin genuinely reckoned with, not waved past, even where forgiveness is granted. Isolating comfort from holiness produces a God who only ever affirms, which the Psalter itself will not permit.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that thou answeredst in the Psalms is always covenantal, addressed to the LORD who has bound himself to his people by promise, never a generic cosmic responsiveness detached from his own character and law.
roots_summary: The archaic -edst ending on answeredst belongs to the same grammatical family as strengthenedst in the same verse, the Authorized Version's consistent marker of the second-person singular past whenever thou is addressed in prayer.
roots_lines: Answeredst in Psalm 99 recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel among those the LORD heard and answered.
The same verse pairs being answered with being forgiven and with sin's consequence not waived.
Answeredst in Psalm 138 turns the same testimony personal, tied to an inward strengthening.
Both psalms use the archaic -edst form only when the LORD himself is the one being addressed.
The pattern models prayer that remembers specific answers rather than speaking only in generalities.
usage: Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God — the Psalter's memory of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel heard.
Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance — grace held with holiness.
In the day when I cried thou answeredst me — personal testimony of prayer heard and felt.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of COVER)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of cover, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version, appearing in contexts as different as creation and covenant unfaithfulness.
biblical_def:
Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment. Tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them.

Coveredst names two opposite kinds of covering. Psalm 104's creation hymn recalls the earth's earliest state, when thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment, the waters not yet gathered into their bounds — a covering the LORD himself later lifts at his rebuke, so the mountains ascend and the valleys descend to the place he founded for them. Ezekiel's oracle against Jerusalem, addressed to her under the figure of an unfaithful wife, uses the identical verb for a covering of an entirely different order: tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them, the gifts the LORD himself gave her — fine linen, silk, embroidered work — spent instead on idols. One covering is the LORD's own sovereign act over creation, undone and remade at his word; the other is a covenant people's misuse of the LORD's own gifts to clothe her unfaithfulness. The same verb, in two mouths, measures the distance between the Creator's ordering hand and a bride's betrayal of him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COVER: to overspread with something; to hide from view; here in the archaic second-person singular past, coveredst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: COVER, v.t. To overspread the surface of a thing with another substance.
COVER, v.t. To hide; to conceal from view or knowledge.
COVEREDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as answeredst.
In Psalm 104 the word names God's own sovereign covering and uncovering of the earth at creation.
In Ezekiel 16 the same word names Jerusalem's misuse of God-given gifts to clothe her idolatry.
scriptures: Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment: the waters stood above the mountains.
And tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them: and thou hast set mine oil and mine incense before them.
corruption_summary: Reading Ezekiel 16's marriage-and-adultery figure as merely archaic patriarchal imagery, rather than the LORD's own chosen figure for covenant unfaithfulness, mutes the oracle's central charge — that Jerusalem's idolatry is spiritual adultery against a real covenant bond.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading embarrassed by Ezekiel 16's marital and bodily imagery can pass quickly over tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them as mere ancient color, missing that the chapter's entire force depends on this covering being a betrayal — gifts of covenant love turned to clothe rival gods. The oracle names the sin precisely because the relationship it violates is precisely intimate.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Psalm 104's coveredst shows the same God who can spread a covering of waters over the whole earth and lift it again at his rebuke — the LORD of Ezekiel 16's jealous covenant love is the same LORD who sovereignly ordered creation in Psalm 104, holiness and power united in one character.
roots_summary: The two occurrences frame coveredst at opposite ends of biblical theology: God's sovereign covering of the deep at creation (Psalm 104), and a covenant people's covering of their idols with his own gifts (Ezekiel 16), the same verb carrying blessing in one mouth and indictment in the other.
roots_lines: Coveredst in Psalm 104 recalls creation's early state, waters standing above the mountains.
The same psalm shows that covering lifted at God's rebuke, the waters set within fixed bounds.
Coveredst in Ezekiel 16 names Jerusalem clothing her idols with the LORD's own gifts of love.
Ezekiel's whole oracle depends on the covenant-marriage figure this covering violates.
Both occurrences show sovereignty and covering as inseparable divine and covenantal themes.
usage: Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment — creation's early state before the waters were bounded.
The waters stood above the mountains — until lifted at the LORD's rebuke (Psalm 104:7-9).
Tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them — Jerusalem clothing idols with God's own gifts.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of CURSE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of curse, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
The silver, about which thou cursedst. The fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away.

Cursedst appears twice, and both times names a curse that finds its mark. Micah's mother, in the strange domestic episode that opens Judges 17, pronounces a curse over eleven hundred shekels of silver stolen from her; her son confesses it was he, about which thou cursedst — the curse working exactly as spoken, driving a guilty conscience to confession even before the idol the silver later becomes is made. Peter's word to Christ is entirely different in kind: Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away, Jesus' acted parable against Israel's fruitless religion (Mark 11:12-14) shown to have taken immediate, visible effect. One curse is a mother's spoken word finding its way to a thief's conscience; the other is the Son of God's spoken word withering a tree to the root overnight. Together they testify that a curse rightly pronounced, whether by a grieving mother or by the Lord of the fig tree, does not return void.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CURSE: to invoke evil upon; to imprecate; here in the archaic second-person singular past, cursedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: CURSE, v.t. To invoke evil upon; to imprecate evil or injury against.
CURSE, n. A malediction; the expression of a wish of evil against a person.
CURSEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as spakest.
In Judges 17 the word names a mother's spoken curse over stolen silver, later confessed to.
In Mark 11 the same word names Christ's spoken curse against a fruitless fig tree, visibly fulfilled.
scriptures: Jdg 17:2

And he said unto his mother, The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from thee, about which thou cursedst, and spakest of also in mine ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it. And his mother said, Blessed be thou of the LORD, my son.
And Peter calling to remembrance saith unto him, Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away.
corruption_summary: Modern sensibility treats Christ's cursing of the fig tree as an embarrassing display of temper rather than a deliberate acted parable; the Gospel's own placement of the episode around the temple's cleansing shows it is a sign-act of judgment on fruitless religion, not an impulsive outburst.
corruption_paragraphs: Some readings, uncomfortable with a miracle of destruction rather than healing, treat the fig tree that thou cursedst is withered away as an odd or petulant moment best minimized. Mark deliberately frames the fig-tree curse around the temple cleansing (Mark 11:12-21), so the withered tree becomes a sign of judgment on a temple system bearing leaves of religious activity without the fruit God actually required.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Judges 17's own quieter witness alongside Mark's: a curse rightly pronounced, whether an ordinary mother's over stolen silver or the Son of God's over a fruitless tree, is never an empty form of words but reaches its object.
roots_summary: The two occurrences of cursedst stand nineteen centuries and two Testaments apart, yet both testify to the same principle: a curse spoken with real authority, whether a mother's grief or the Lord's own judgment, accomplishes what it declares.
roots_lines: Cursedst in Judges 17 names a mother's curse over stolen silver, later confessed to by her own son.
The confession itself, about which thou cursedst, shows the curse working on a guilty conscience.
Cursedst in Mark 11 names Christ's spoken judgment against a fig tree bearing leaves but no fruit.
Mark frames the fig tree's cursing around the temple's cleansing as one connected acted parable.
Both occurrences show a pronounced curse reaching its mark rather than passing as empty words.
usage: The silver, about which thou cursedst — a mother's curse reaching a thief's conscience in Judges 17.
The fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away — Peter's report of Christ's acted parable fulfilled.
Framed around the temple's cleansing — the fig tree as a sign against fruitless religion.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of FORGIVE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of forgive, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version, from Anglo-Saxon forgiefan, to give fully, to give up entirely.
biblical_def:
Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.

Forgavest is the Psalter's word for the exact moment confession meets mercy. Psalm 99 sets it beside a harder companion clause: a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions, holding forgiveness and just consequence together rather than letting one cancel the other. Psalm 32, David's own confession psalm, narrates the sequence with more intimacy: I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid; I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD, and — with no gap, no probation, no delay — thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. The verb's placement is the theology: forgiveness in Scripture follows confession as immediately as the sentence itself, not because sin is small but because the LORD who forgives is the same LORD whose mercy the whole Psalter has already tested and found sure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FORGIVE: to pardon; to remit an offense; here in the archaic second-person singular past, forgavest, addressed to thou in confession and praise.
webster_full: FORGIVE, v.t. To pardon; to remit, as an offense, debt, or penalty.
FORGIVE, v.t. To cease to feel resentment against, on account of wrong committed.
FORGAVEST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as gavest, from GIVE.
In Psalm 99 forgiveness stands beside, not against, just consequence for sin.
In Psalm 32 forgiveness follows confession immediately, within the same breath of the psalm.
scriptures: Psa 99:8
Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions.
Psa 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
corruption_summary: Cheap-grace readings collapse forgavest into a blanket, consequence-free acceptance detached from confession; Psalm 32 shows forgiveness following genuine acknowledgment of sin, and Psalm 99 shows it standing alongside real temporal consequence, neither psalm supporting forgiveness without repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic-culture misreading treats thou forgavest as evidence that God's acceptance requires nothing from the one forgiven, no acknowledgment, no confession, no genuine turning from sin. Psalm 32 places I acknowledged my sin unto thee directly before thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin — forgiveness real and immediate, but never apart from confession honestly made.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Psalm 99's own balance: forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions shows that forgiveness of guilt and temporal consequence for sin are not opposites in Scripture's own accounting, however uncomfortable that pairing is to a flattened modern notion of grace.
roots_summary: Forgavest shares its archaic -st ending with gavest, both drawn from the same root verb give — forgive being, at its Anglo-Saxon root, to give up entirely, to give fully and finally, the etymology itself picturing debt cancelled rather than merely excused.
roots_lines: Forgavest in Psalm 99 stands beside a sobering companion clause about consequence still borne.
Forgavest in Psalm 32 follows immediately after confession honestly and fully made.
The Anglo-Saxon root forgiefan pictures forgiveness as giving up a debt entirely, not excusing it.
Both psalms place forgavest in direct address to God, never as an abstract theological claim.
The word's placement in each psalm is itself the doctrine: confession precedes, forgiveness follows.
usage: Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance — mercy and consequence held together.
I acknowledged my sin unto thee... and thou forgavest — David's confession psalm, Psalm 32.
I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD — the pattern forgiveness in Scripture always follows.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of SIT)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of sit, formed with the -est ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version — thou satest, one throne of judgment, one seat of harlotry.
biblical_def:
Thou satest in the throne judging right. Satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it.

Satest names two seats that could not be more opposed. David's psalm of thanksgiving praises the LORD's own righteous rule: thou satest in the throne judging right, the LORD himself pictured as judge, his verdicts against the heathen and the wicked already accomplished and celebrated in the same breath. Ezekiel's oracle against Jerusalem, under the figure of the unfaithful sister Aholibah, uses the identical verb for an entirely different seat: satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it, decked with the LORD's own incense and oil, but spread now for idolatrous lovers rather than for him. Set together, the two thrones expose the choice every covenant heart faces: to sit under the LORD's own righteous judgment as David does, gladly, or to seat oneself amid stolen gifts turned to false worship, as Jerusalem is charged with doing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SIT: to rest upon the buttocks; to be placed, as on a seat, throne, or bed; here in the archaic second-person singular past, satest, addressed to thou.
webster_full: SIT, v.i. To rest on the buttocks, as men or animals; to be seated.
SIT, v.i. To occupy a seat of office, as a judge, king, or ruler.
SATEST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -est, as knewest.
In Psalm 9 the word pictures the LORD enthroned as righteous judge over the nations.
In Ezekiel 23 the same word pictures a covenant people's idolatrous seat, decked with stolen gifts.
scriptures: Psa 9:4
For thou hast maintained my right and my cause; thou satest in the throne judging right.
And satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it, whereupon thou hast set mine incense and mine oil.
corruption_summary: A generic, uncritical celebration of divine judgment as always comforting, without reckoning that the same judging throne of Psalm 9 stands ready to expose the idolatrous seat of Ezekiel 23, flattens the sober warning Ezekiel's oracle is meant to deliver to a covenant people, not only to outsiders.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading that keeps thou satest in the throne judging right purely as personal comfort, without letting it also stand as warning, misses that the LORD who judges right in Psalm 9 is the same LORD whose gifts — incense and oil — are stolen for the idolatrous bed of Ezekiel 23. The judging throne is not only for enemies outside the covenant; it examines the covenant people's own use of what he has given them.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Psalm 9's confidence — thou satest in the throne judging right — is available only to those who have not, like the figure in Ezekiel 23, taken the LORD's own gifts and turned them to serve another throne.
roots_summary: The archaic -est ending on satest belongs to the same family as answeredst and stoodest, and its placement in these two very different scenes — a righteous throne, an idolatrous bed — shows the Authorized Version using one grammatical form across the widest range of biblical subject matter.
roots_lines: Satest in Psalm 9 pictures the LORD enthroned as righteous judge over the heathen and the wicked.
The psalm ties this throne directly to David's own right and cause being maintained.
Satest in Ezekiel 23 pictures a covenant people's idolatrous seat, spread with the LORD's stolen gifts.
Both occurrences involve a seat prepared and gifts set before it, one holy, one corrupted.
Ezekiel's oracle addresses Jerusalem under the figure of Aholibah, sister to Samaria's Aholah.
usage: Thou satest in the throne judging right — the LORD's righteous rule celebrated in Psalm 9.
Thou hast maintained my right and my cause — the ground of confidence in that righteous throne.
Satest upon a stately bed... whereupon thou hast set mine incense and mine oil — Jerusalem's idolatrous seat.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon compound of middle + -most, a native English superlative ending (as in utmost, foremost) rather than the Latinate -est, appearing in the Authorized Version only in Ezekiel's temple-vision architecture.
biblical_def:
The galleries were higher than these... than the middlemost of the building. Therefore the building was straitened more than the lowest and the middlemost from the ground.

Middlemost belongs entirely to Ezekiel's detailed vision of a restored temple, measured chamber by chamber, story by story, in careful architectural language unlike almost anything else in the prophets. Twice the word names the middle story of a three-storied structure of priests' chambers, set apart for holy use, the text distinguishing lowest, middlemost, and (by implication) highest with the same precision a builder would use, not the loose approximation of ordinary narrative. This exactness is itself part of Ezekiel's message: after the temple's defilement and destruction, the vision answers with a structure measured to the cubit, nothing vague or improvised about the holiness it houses. Middlemost is a small word doing a large work — insisting that when the LORD rebuilds what sin has ruined, the rebuilding is exact, not approximate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from MIDDLE + -MOST: situated equally distant from the extremes; the superlative of middle, formed with the native English -most ending rather than -est.
webster_full: MIDDLE, a. Equally distant from the extremes; intervening.
-MOST, a native English superlative suffix, as in utmost, foremost, hindmost.
MIDDLEMOST, a. Situated in the exact middle among more than two; the superlative of middle.
In Ezekiel 42 the word specifies the middle of three stories of priests' chambers.
The precision of lowest, middlemost, and highest matches the vision's exact, measured character.
scriptures: Eze 42:5
Now the upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these, than the lower, and than the middlemost of the building.
Eze 42:6
For they were in three stories, but had not pillars as the pillars of the courts: therefore the building was straitened more than the lowest and the middlemost from the ground.
corruption_summary: Skeptical scholarship treats Ezekiel's exact temple measurements, middlemost story included, as either a late priestly literary fiction or an unrealizable utopian blueprint never meant to be built; the text presents the vision with the same historical seriousness as the earlier temple it replaces.
corruption_paragraphs: Approaches that read Ezekiel 40-48 purely as symbolic or utopian literature can treat details like the middlemost story's dimensions as decorative precision with no real referent, whether historical, future, or otherwise. The prophet is given the vision by direct divine agency, measured by a man with a measuring reed (Eze 40:3), presented with the same seriousness as any historical building account in the Old Testament.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's own restoration of what sin has ruined is never careless — the middlemost chamber, measured as precisely as the lowest and the highest, testifies that holiness rebuilt is holiness ordered to the smallest detail, not a vague or general promise.
roots_summary: Middlemost preserves the Anglo-Saxon -most superlative pattern (foremost, utmost, hindmost, uttermost) rather than the more common Latinate -est ending, one of several native English superlative forms the Authorized Version retains where modern usage has largely abandoned them.
roots_lines: Middlemost appears only in Ezekiel's detailed vision of the restored temple's priestly chambers.
Both occurrences distinguish the middlemost story from the lower and the higher precisely.
The word's -most ending places it among other native English superlatives like utmost and foremost.
Ezekiel's temple vision is introduced by a man with a measuring reed, exact rather than symbolic.
The precision of the architecture matches the seriousness with which the whole vision is presented.
usage: The galleries were higher than these, than the lower, and than the middlemost — Ezekiel's exact temple vision.
The building was straitened more than the lowest and the middlemost from the ground — precise measurement.
Measured with a measuring reed — the seriousness with which the whole restored temple is presented (Eze 40:3).

etymology: Anglo-Saxon norð (north) + -ern, an adjective-forming suffix denoting direction — northern names the compass-quarter from which Scripture's great invading powers characteristically come.
biblical_def:
Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel? I will remove far off from you the northern army.

Northern in the Authorized Version marks a fixed prophetic direction, the quarter from which judgment and invasion characteristically come upon Israel and Judah, since Mesopotamian and later powers approached the land from the north rather than across the intervening desert to the east. Jeremiah's brief oracle asks, almost rhetorically, shall iron break the northern iron and the steel — a picture of Judah's own supposed strength measured against an invader as hard as iron, the answer implied to be no, not by any strength Judah herself possesses. Joel's locust-plague oracle applies the same compass-word to an army of a different kind, the northern army, whose devastation the LORD promises finally to remove far off, driven into a barren and desolate land. Northern thus gathers, in two words, both the direction from which Scripture's judgments typically arrive and the LORD's own sovereign power to reverse them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), NORTHERN: pertaining to the north; being in the north, or nearer to that point than to the east or west.
webster_full: NORTHERN, a. Pertaining to the north; being in the north.
NORTHERN, a. In a direction toward the north; northerly.
Used in Scripture chiefly of invading powers approaching Israel and Judah from Mesopotamia.
In Jeremiah 15 the word describes an iron as hard as the invader Judah cannot resist by her own strength.
In Joel 2 the same word describes a locust army the LORD himself promises to remove and destroy.
scriptures: Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?
Joe 2:20

But I will remove far off from you the northern army, and will drive him into a land barren and desolate, with his face toward the east sea, and his hinder part toward the utmost sea, and his stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up, because he hath done great things.
corruption_summary: Purely meteorological or agricultural readings of Joel's locust plague, detached from the book's own theological frame, miss that the northern army is presented throughout as an instrument of the LORD's own hand, removed by his hand as surely as it was sent by it.
corruption_paragraphs: An approach that reads Joel's locusts as simply a natural disaster narrated in vivid poetic language can lose the book's own insistence that the northern army, whether locusts or a literal military invader or both, acts as the LORD's own instrument of judgment, and is removed only because the LORD himself removes it, not because of any natural cycle running its course.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own rhetorical question: shall iron break the northern iron and the steel — Judah's confidence in her own strength against the coming invader is exposed as false confidence, the same lesson Deuteronomy 28's trustedst already pronounced against fenced walls.
roots_summary: The northern direction recurs across the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Zephaniah) as the standing quarter of judgment, since Assyria and Babylon, though east of Israel, invaded by the Fertile Crescent's northern arc rather than the desert route.
roots_lines: Northern in Jeremiah 15 names an invader as hard as iron, against which Judah's own strength fails.
Northern in Joel 2 names a devastating army, whether locust or military or both in one figure.
In both books the northern power acts as an instrument sent, and later removed, by the LORD's own hand.
The compass-direction reflects the actual invasion route of Mesopotamian powers into Israel and Judah.
Joel's promise to remove the northern army models the LORD reversing judgment once repentance is real.
usage: Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel — Judah's own strength exposed as inadequate.
I will remove far off from you the northern army — the LORD's promise to reverse the judgment he sent.
His stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up — the invader's total, visible destruction.

etymology: Compound of there + out, one of a family of archaic English compound adverbs (thereof, therein, thereby, thereout) the Authorized Version uses freely and modern English has largely retired.
biblical_def:
He shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof. There came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again.

Thereout names a taking-from or a coming-from that is precise about its source. Leviticus's instructions for the meat offering specify that the priest shall take thereout his handful of the flour, a portion drawn out of the whole offering as a memorial burned upon the altar, the rest reserved for the priests — the word marking exactly where the handful comes from, not merely that a handful is taken. Judges uses the same word for water bursting from the hollow place God clave in the jaw at Lehi to revive the exhausted Samson: there came water thereout, drink drawn out from a source the text is careful to locate precisely, an unglamorous rock rather than any resource of Samson's own. In both cases thereout insists that what is drawn out — flour for the LORD's altar, water for Samson's parched throat — comes from a specific, named source, not from nowhere.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), THEREOUT: out of that place, thing, or number; out from that source specifically named.
webster_full: THEREOUT, adv. Out of that; out of that place or thing.
One of a family of archaic compound adverbs (thereof, therein, thereby, thereout, thereupon) in the Authorized Version.
In Leviticus 2 the word specifies the exact source of the priest's memorial handful of flour.
In Judges 15 the word specifies the exact source of the water that revives the exhausted Samson.
Largely displaced in modern English by prepositional phrases such as out of it or from there.
scriptures: Lev 2:2

And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar, to be an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD:

But God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw, and there came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived: wherefore he called the name thereof Enhakkore, which is in Lehi unto this day.
corruption_summary: Reading Samson's revival at Lehi as simply a folk legend about a spring's origin misses that the text names the place Enhakkore, the well of him that cried, specifically to memorialize God's answer to a specific prayer of a specific exhausted man, not to explain a natural landmark in general.
corruption_paragraphs: A skeptical reading treats there came water thereout as an etiological folk tale explaining a spring's name, detached from any real answer to prayer. The narrative is explicit that Samson cried unto the LORD just before, and the water bursts from the ground God himself cleaves open in direct, immediate response, the place named afterward specifically to memorialize that answered prayer.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Leviticus's own quiet lesson in the meat offering: what is taken thereout, the priest's handful drawn precisely from the whole, is burned first as the LORD's portion before anything else is used, ordinary flour made an offering of a sweet savour by exact, obedient handling.
roots_summary: Thereout belongs to a whole family of English compound adverbs built on there (thereof, therein, thereby, thereout, thereupon, thereafter), once common and precise, now largely replaced in ordinary speech by prepositional phrases.
roots_lines: Thereout in Leviticus 2 specifies the priest's memorial handful as drawn from the whole meat offering.
The handful taken thereout is burned first as the LORD's own portion, the rest reserved for the priests.
Thereout in Judges 15 specifies the water that revives Samson as coming from a place God himself cleaves.
The place is named Enhakkore afterward specifically to memorialize this answer to prayer.
Both occurrences use thereout to name a precise source rather than a vague or general one.
usage: He shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof — the priest's memorial portion, precisely sourced.
There came water thereout — the spring God opens to revive the exhausted Samson at Lehi.
He called the name thereof Enhakkore — a place named to memorialize a specific answered prayer.

pos: v. (archaic 3rd pers. sing. pres., of OWN)
etymology: Archaic third-person singular present of own, formed with the -eth ending used throughout the Authorized Version, from Anglo-Saxon agnian, to possess or claim as one's own.
biblical_def:
He that owneth the house shall come and tell the priest. The man that owneth this girdle.

Owneth in Scripture is a word of accountable possession, never merely casual belonging. Leviticus's law for a house afflicted with the plague of leprosy requires that he that owneth the house shall come and tell the priest, saying, it seemeth to me there is as it were a plague in the house — ownership here obligates disclosure, not concealment, the owner responsible to report the very defect he might be tempted to hide for the sake of the house's value. Agabus, binding his own hands and feet with Paul's girdle at Caesarea, prophesies in nearly identical grammar that the Jews at Jerusalem shall bind the man that owneth this girdle, Paul himself named by what belongs to him rather than by name alone. Both occurrences make the same quiet point: to own a thing in Scripture is to be bound to it, answerable for it, identified by it — never a possession without responsibility attached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from OWN: to hold as property; to possess; to acknowledge as belonging to oneself; here in the archaic third-person singular present, owneth, as in giveth, walketh.
webster_full: OWN, v.t. To hold as property; to have the legal or rightful title to.
OWN, v.t. To acknowledge; to confess as belonging to, or as being of, oneself.
OWNETH, the archaic third-person singular present, formed with -eth, as giveth, walketh.
In Leviticus 14 the word obligates an owner to disclose, not conceal, a defect in his own house.
In Acts 21 the word identifies Paul by the girdle that belongs to him, in Agabus's own prophecy.
scriptures: And he that owneth the house shall come and tell the priest, saying, It seemeth to me there is as it were a plague in the house:

And when he was come unto us, he took Paul's girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: A consumer-culture instinct treats ownership as pure entitlement, use without accountability; Leviticus 14 binds ownership to obligatory disclosure of defect, a pattern of accountable stewardship rather than unencumbered possession.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern property instinct assumes an owner's chief interest is protecting the value of what he owns, concealing defects where possible. The law of the leprous house inverts this instinct entirely: he that owneth the house is commanded to report the very plague that threatens the house's worth, ownership under the law functioning as stewardship accountable to the priest and, behind him, to the LORD, not as private entitlement to manage as one pleases.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Agabus's own prophetic act at Caesarea: Paul is identified by what owneth him, the girdle marking him out for binding, a small enacted parable of the larger truth that Paul is not his own, bought with a price, and goes to Jerusalem bound in every sense before the Jews ever lay a hand on him.
roots_summary: Owneth's archaic -eth ending follows the standard Authorized Version pattern of the third-person singular present, and its Anglo-Saxon root agnian (to claim as one's own) underlies both the verb own and the noun owner, of accountable possession rather than bare use.
roots_lines: Owneth in Leviticus 14 obligates a house's owner to report, not conceal, a defect God's law requires disclosed.
The law treats ownership under the covenant as a form of stewardship accountable to the priest.
Owneth in Acts 21 identifies Paul by the girdle Agabus binds, prophesying his coming arrest.
Agabus's acted prophecy, like the Old Testament prophets' sign-acts, embodies the word before it is fulfilled.
Both occurrences tie owneth to accountability rather than to unencumbered private entitlement.
usage: He that owneth the house shall come and tell the priest — accountable disclosure required of an owner.
It seemeth to me there is as it were a plague in the house — the owner's own obligatory report.
The man that owneth this girdle — Agabus's prophetic sign identifying Paul before his arrest.

pos: v. (archaic 3rd pers. sing. pres., of FORESEE)
etymology: Fore- (before) + see, formed with the archaic -eth ending used throughout the Authorized Version — a compound as old as Anglo-Saxon foreseon, to see beforehand.
biblical_def:
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.

Foreseeth belongs to Proverbs' repeated teaching on prudence, and Scripture underscores the lesson by giving it twice, word for word, in two separate collections within the same book. A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished — the whole of practical wisdom compressed into one antithesis. Foresight here is not fearful anxiety but sober realism, the willingness to reckon honestly with danger before it arrives rather than after, and to take the humble, unglamorous action — hideth himself — that danger foreseen actually calls for. The simple man's failure is not a lack of information but a lack of the will to act on what could have been foreseen; he passes on exactly where the prudent man turns aside, and the consequence, are punished, falls on presumption rather than on ignorance alone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FORESEE: to see or know beforehand; to perceive an event before it happens, by means of present signs; here in the archaic third-person singular present, foreseeth.
webster_full: FORESEE, v.t. To see or know beforehand; to have prescience of.
FORESEE, v.t. To perceive an event before it takes place, by reasoning on causes.
FORESEETH, the archaic third-person singular present, formed with -eth, as walketh, doeth.
The proverb pairs foreseeth with hideth, prudent perception joined to prudent action.
The identical proverb appears twice in the book, at Proverbs 22:3 and Proverbs 27:12.
scriptures: Pro 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the simple pass on, and are punished.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic culture that treats all anticipation of danger as anxiety to be managed away misreads foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself as fearfulness; Proverbs commends this foresight as prudence, the opposite virtue from the presumption of the simple who pass on regardless.
corruption_paragraphs: Some contemporary readings, suspicious of any counsel to anticipate danger, treat foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself as excessive caution or even cowardice, prizing instead a bold refusal to consider consequences. Proverbs names the opposite behavior, passing on regardless of foreseeable danger, as the mark of the simple who are punished, not as courage but as folly.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's own repetition of this exact proverb, word for word, in two different collections within Proverbs is itself a teaching device — wisdom worth saying twice, so that a hearer who missed it in chapter 22 meets it again, unaltered, in chapter 27.
roots_summary: Foreseeth is a fore- compound, the same prefix seen in foreknow and foreordain, joined here to see rather than to a more theologically loaded verb, keeping the proverb's focus on ordinary practical perception rather than divine foreknowledge.
roots_lines: Foreseeth pairs with hideth in both occurrences, prudent perception joined to prudent action.
The proverb's antithesis sets the prudent man's foresight against the simple man's presumption.
The identical wording appears twice in Proverbs, at 22:3 and again at 27:12, without variation.
The fore- prefix (before) is the same element found in foreknow, foreordain, and forewarn.
The proverb concerns ordinary practical wisdom, not the specialized doctrine of divine foreknowledge.
usage: A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself — Proverbs' repeated teaching on practical wisdom.
But the simple pass on, and are punished — presumption named as folly, not courage.
Repeated word for word at Proverbs 22:3 and 27:12 — wisdom worth saying twice.
